project.title: Running title: Highly pure isolation of small extracellular vesicles from bovine plasma Title: Technical note: Efficient enrichment of plasma-derived extracellular vesicles from small volumes of bovine blood
project.projectDescription: This study presents a scalable method for isolating small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) according to MISEV (minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles) guidelines from 4 mL of bovine plasma while achieving a high purity suitable for proteomics analysis. The protocol combines ultracentrifugation (UC), size-exclusion chromatography (SEC), and ultrafiltration (UF) to minimize contamination by lipoproteins and free proteins. The purified sEVs were characterized through transmission electron microscopy (TEM), tunable resistive pulse sensing (TRPS), dynamic light scattering (DLS), and flow cytometry (FC), assessing particle size, morphology, and the presence of membrane markers such as CD9. The purity assessed by the particle-to-protein ratio (4.8 × 10⁸ particles/µg in average) was improved (× 10) compared to the previous protocol. Mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) and Parallel Reaction Monitoring (PRM) identified 417 proteins, 93% of which are referenced in sEVs databases. Specific markers of sEVs have been identified including cytosolic (HSPA8, SDCBP, ACT, TUB, and GAPDH) and membrane (CD9 and CD81) Markers. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis revealed an enrichment of sEVs proteins. This study demonstrates that this sEVs enrichment protocol is well-suited for small plasma volumes. These results pave the way for future studies of biomarker research on animal health and performance.
project.sampleProcessingProtocol: Blood Collection and Plasma Preparation In 2021, bovine blood was collected when animals reached ~530 kg, early morning before feeding, after overnight fasting to reduce lipoproteins interfering with extracellular vesicle (EV) analysis. Samples were drawn by jugular venipuncture into EDTA tubes (Vacutainer® system), kept on ice, and processed within 1.5 h. Plasma was obtained by centrifugation (3,000 g, 15 min, 4 °C), yielding cell-free supernatants stored at –80 °C until vesicle isolation. Extraction, Purification, and Concentration of Small Extracellular Vesicles (sEVs) Plasma samples were thawed at 4 °C, diluted 1:1 with filtered DPBS, and sequentially centrifuged (2,000 g, 30 min ×2; 12,000 g, 45 min, 4 °C) to remove debris. Supernatants were filtered (0.22 µm) to exclude particles >220 nm, then ultracentrifuged (120,000 g, 2 h, 4 °C). Pellets were resuspended in DPBS overnight. To improve purity and minimize lipoproteins, suspensions were processed through qEV70 Gen2 size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) columns: the first 2 mL was discarded, and the following 1.5 mL, defined as the Particle Collection Volume (PCV), was retained as the sEV-rich fraction. Columns were washed (NaOH, DPBS) and reused up to three times. From each PCV, 50 µL was used for immediate characterization (TRPS, DLS, flow cytometry), while 150 µL per animal was pooled for electron microscopy. Final concentration was achieved with 10 kDa Amicon filters (three washes). The resulting 100 µL concentrate was divided into 20 µL aliquots and stored at –20 °C. Characterization of sEVs Multiple complementary techniques validated vesicle quality. Morphology was confirmed by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) after fixation, negative staining (UranyLess), and imaging at 80 kV. Particle size and concentration were measured with Tunable Resistive Pulse Sensing (TRPS, qNano Gold, NP150 nanopores), calibrated with silica beads. At least 500 particle counts per run ensured accurate profiles. Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) provided hydrodynamic size and polydispersity indices from Brownian motion, complementing TRPS. Nano-Flow Cytometry (NanoFCM) combined sizing with molecular marker detection. Pooled sEVs were incubated with FITC-labeled anti-CD9 antibodies (with isotype controls), ultracentrifuged to remove unbound antibodies, and analyzed to quantify CD9-positive vesicles along with concentration and size distributions. Protein Quantification, Purity Estimation, and Peptide Preparation (S-Trap Method) Protein content of sEVs was measured using a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay, providing inputs for downstream proteomics (10 µg required). Purity was assessed by particle-to-protein ratios, higher values indicating better enrichment. Particle counts were from TRPS, protein mass from BCA. For proteomics, 10 µg protein per preparation was processed via the S-Trap protocol. Proteins were solubilized in SDS buffer, reduced with DTT, alkylated with iodoacetamide, then acidified and captured in S-Trap microcolumns. After washes, proteins were digested overnight with trypsin (1:50). Peptides were eluted sequentially with TEAB, formic acid, and acetonitrile, dried by vacuum concentration, resuspended in formic acid with isotopically labeled standards, transferred to HPLC vials, and stored at –20 °C. Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics Peptides were analyzed using nano-LC-MS/MS on an Ultimate 3000 HPLC coupled to an Orbitrap QExactive HF-X mass spectrometer. Samples were concentrated/desalted on a C18 pre-column, separated on a long C18 column with an acetonitrile gradient, and ionized by positive-mode electrospray. Two acquisition methods were used: • Individual samples (Top-18 DDA): Full MS scans followed by MS/MS of the 18 most abundant ions, maximizing proteome depth. • Pooled samples (Top-15 DDA + PRM): Data-dependent acquisition combined with targeted Parallel Reaction Monitoring (PRM). PRM targeted established sEV markers (CD9, CD81, HSPs, TSG101) using peptide libraries built in Skyline.
project.dataProcessingProtocol: The peptide MS/MS spectra were processed using Progenesis QI (v4.2, Nonlinear Dynamics). Runs were automatically aligned against a reference, and detected ions were exported as mgf files to Mascot Server 3.1. Searches were performed against the ref_bos_taurus_241029 database (59,261 sequences) with stringent parameters: precursor mass tolerance of 10 ppm, fragment mass tolerance of 0.02 Da, allowance of two trypsin missed cleavages, and variable modifications including carbamidomethylation (C), oxidation (M), and deamidation (NQ). Proteins were considered valid with at least two peptides, a false discovery rate (FDR) of 1% (p < 0.02), and a Mascot ion score above 34. This yielded 772 proteins identified with at least one peptide. For gene ontology (GO) analysis, only proteins supported by two or more significant peptide sequences (462 in total) were retained. Contaminants flagged by Mascot, as well as apolipoproteins (APO) known to originate from lipoproteins, were excluded. The resulting dataset comprised 406 proteins. Human homologs were determined using ProteINSIDE (Kaspric et al., 2015) based on bovine gene names. If unsuccessful, BLASTp alignments against the human proteome were performed. Selection favored hits with the highest alignment coverage when multiple candidates shared identical e-values. In unresolved cases, multiple gene names were retained; if no reliable alignment was achieved, no homolog was assigned. Finally, enrichment analysis of GO terms was performed using ProteINSIDE and ShinyGO v0.82 (Ge et al., 2020), focusing specifically on Cellular Components (CC). Only results with FDR < 0.01 were considered significant.
